Published: 10 minutes ago Photo by Claudia Seidensticker via Pexels Chinese brands shift overseas focus to store productivity, localisation Hong Kong and Southeast Asia are key markets for growth.
Chinese brands are shifting their overseas expansion strategies from rapid store openings to store productivity, localisation, and brand building as competition and margin pressure intensify in mainland China.
Hong Kong and Southeast Asia have emerged as key markets for Chinese retailers seeking international growth, according to Savills' Inside Occupier Strategy - Retail report. However, expansion strategies are becoming more targeted, with brands reviewing underperforming locations, upgrading flagship stores and investing in local operating capabilities.
The expansion is also spreading beyond food and beverage (F&B) and value retail into fashion, jewellery, beauty and lifestyle. Brands are increasingly using design, cultural identity and customer experiences to differentiate themselves beyond competitive pricing.
Physical stores remain central to this strategy. Retailers are using outlets as showrooms and social destinations to demonstrate product quality, engage customers and direct online audiences towards in-store purchases.
Southeast Asia offers Chinese brands opportunities to expand their customer base, supported by rising incomes, urbanisation and demand for affordable-premium products. However, differences in consumer behaviour, regulations, purchasing power and logistics require market-specific strategies.
Vietnam and Indonesia offer opportunities for larger-scale expansion, whilst Singapore serves as a platform for brand positioning and testing store formats. Malaysia can help brands develop operational capabilities before expanding further across the region.
Retail sales have generally outpaced rents across selected cities since early 2023. Bangkok recorded the strongest increase in the sales-to-rent index, followed by improving conditions in Ho Chi Minh City and Kuala Lumpur. Jakarta and Singapore recorded more moderate movements.
In Vietnam, tourism, urban development and rising purchasing power are supporting retail demand. In Jakarta, limited prime retail supply and high occupancy in stronger shopping centres favour established retail locations. Thailand offers opportunities in tourism-driven retail, particularly in wellness, healthcare, entertainment and dining.
However, limited prime space in Singapore, competition for locations in Thailand and uneven market transparency in Vietnam and Indonesia can complicate expansion. Retailers must assess local demand, occupancy costs and partner capabilities before opening new stores.
Chinese brands are using Hong Kong to strengthen their positioning, test premium store formats and reach local consumers, mainland Chinese visitors and international tourists.
Retail sales in the city recorded 15 consecutive months of year-on-year growth from May 2025 to July 2026. Visitors from the Netherlands, the UK, the US, and Australia also recorded relatively high spending.
Brands are opening prominent flagship stores, entering established regional shopping centres and using pop-ups to test demand before making larger investments. Click-and-collect, ship-from-store and cross-channel returns are also extending the role of physical stores beyond direct sales.
However, high rents, labour expenses and fit-out costs raise the sales required to make stores profitable. Brands must choose locations carefully and avoid oversized stores that cannot generate sufficient revenue.
Chinese retailers are investing in local teams, staff training, supply chains, and market-specific products to improve overseas performance.
"International expansion is becoming less about replicating a successful domestic model and more about building the capabilities required to operate locally," the report said.
Local sourcing, halal certification, language capabilities, and after-sales service are amongst the requirements that brands may need to address when entering new markets.
Retailers must also adapt pricing, marketing and customer service to local preferences and regulations. Strong local partners can help them navigate these requirements whilst maintaining consistent operating standards.
Chinese brands are placing greater emphasis on design, product quality, and customer experience to distinguish themselves from competitors.
Stores featuring interactive services, product customisation, limited-edition launches and localised displays can help brands build customer loyalty and strengthen their positioning.
For landlords, productive Chinese tenants can attract new customer groups, refresh tenant mixes, and generate turnover-based rental income.
For retailers, sustainable overseas growth will depend on selecting productive locations, building strong local partnerships and ensuring stores generate enough sales to cover occupancy costs.
The objective is not simply to generate footfall, but to convert attention into affinity, repeat visits and pricing power," Savills said. "Brands that achieve this can progress from being perceived as affordable alternatives to becoming desirable global propositions with a clear identity and loyal customer base."
